query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor oxide‐forming element (e.g. ~0.3–0.5 wt % Al) into the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will induce an in situ nanohierarchical microstructure featuring ultrafine grains and nano‐oxide precipitates. This engineered heterogeneous structure is expected to provide adaptive friction interface protection across the full sliding temperature range by promoting multiple deformation mechanisms at low temperatures and enabling rapid formation of a protective nanocrystalline glaze layer at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous single-phase FCC structure.
generation.intervention: Alloying: addition of a small amount of an oxide-forming element (such as Al) to trigger controlled nanoprecipitation and grain refinement during processing and sliding.
generation.conditions: Reciprocating sliding tests conducted from room temperature up to 800 °C at comparable loads and speeds to prior wear and friction experiments (e.g., as in PMC10456374 and PMC9960858 studies), in an ambient or slightly oxidative environment.
generation.structural_mediator: Development of a nanohierarchical microstructure comprising ultrafine grains and in situ precipitated nano-oxides that act as stress relievers at low temperature and as precursors for a protective nanocrystalline oxide glaze at high temperature.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the heterogeneous microstructure allows for gradient friction stress release through multiple deformation pathways, minimizing adhesive wear. At high temperatures, the nano-oxides promote rapid tribo-oxidation and formation of a dense glaze layer that mitigates adhesive and oxidative wear, thereby stabilizing the friction coefficient.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified CoCrFeNi alloy is predicted to exhibit a consistently lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the entire temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C) compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.baseline: The pristine CoCrFeNi alloy, which under identical sliding conditions shows increased friction and wear rate—particularly at high temperatures due to enhanced adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.boundary: Sliding contact conditions with loads and sliding speeds consistent with those in prior tribological studies, temperature range from ~25 °C to 800 °C, and testing in an environment where limited oxidation occurs (controlled ambient conditions).
generation.uncertainty: The optimal concentration of the oxide-forming element and the detailed evolution kinetics of the nanohierarchical microstructure during sliding remain to be determined. There is also uncertainty about potential changes in other mechanical properties of the alloy due to the addition.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of CoCrFeNi alloy: one in the original composition and one with an added 0.3–0.5 wt % of Al. Process both to ensure similar initial microstructures aside from the intervention. Conduct reciprocating sliding tests under identical loads, sliding speeds, and temperatures (room temperature, intermediate temperature around 400 °C, and high temperature at 800 °C). Characterize the friction coefficient in real time and determine wear volumes post-test via Archard’s law. Use SEM/TEM analysis to verify the existence of the expected nanohierarchical microstructure and the formation of a nanocrystalline oxide glaze layer at high temperatures.
measurements: Real-time coefficient of friction data across the temperature range
Wear volume (mm³) and specific wear rate calculated from sliding tests
Microstructural analyses (SEM/TEM) for grain size, nano-oxide dispersion, and glaze layer formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped CoCrFeNi alloy does not consistently show a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and specific wear rate compared to the unmodified alloy across the tested temperature range, or if the anticipated nanohierarchical microstructure and oxide glaze layer are absent or not sufficiently developed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. We show below that our experiments on HEA can be modeled by a weakening, ε, that grows with the ratio, Λ/Ω, of the healing rate, Λ, relative to the strain-rate, Ω. For sufficiently-low temperatures, it is reasonable to assume that pinning of the dislocations involves activated processes. Consequently, the healing rate, Λ, follows an Arrhenius-like temperature (T) dependence, Λ ~ exp(−B/T), where B is a material-dependent constant. In close analogy to a similar mechanism in polymers, known as time-temperature superposition, one concludes that the relevant parameter for the slip statistics is then Λ/Ω ~ exp(−B/T)/Ω, i.e., similar slip statistics are expected for temperatures, T, and strain-rates, Ω, for which exp(−B/T)/Ω = constant. As discussed in the experimental section, this prediction is consistent with the experimental data (Figures 1, 2, 3).

AbstractA novel metal matrix composite CrMnFeCoNi with Y2O3 as reinforcement phase was designed and manufactured by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering. After sintering at 900 °C for 5 min, the microstructure consisted of a FCC matrix and Y2O3 nanoparticles. The addition of 0.25 wt % Y2O3 increased the room temperature tensile strength of the CrMnFeCoNi base from 868 MPa to 1001 MPa, while the mechanical properties of the addition of 0.5 wt % Y2O3 composite decreased.
